topics.title: print()
topics.summary: Displays a value in the Python output console.
topics.description:
Put **text**, numbers or variables inside the brackets. Strings must be surrounded by quotation marks.

For example, `python:print("Hello!")` displays a greeting.
topics.syntax: Use `python:print("Hello, world!")` to display a message.

topics.title: Comments
topics.summary: Notes in code that Python ignores when the program runs.
topics.description:
Use comments to explain code, leave reminders, or temporarily turn off a line while debugging.

Python ignores anything after `python:#` on that line.
topics.syntax:
```python
# This line is a comment
print("This line runs")
```

topics.title: Debugging
topics.summary: Finding and fixing mistakes so code works as intended.
topics.description: Bugs can be tiny, such as a missing quote, bracket, colon, or indentation. Debugging means reading the error, checking the code carefully, and testing the fix.
topics.syntax:
```python
# Missing the closing quote would cause an error:
print("Hello!")
```

topics.title: Syntax
topics.summary: The exact spelling and punctuation rules a programming language expects.
topics.description:
Python syntax includes brackets after functions, quotation marks around strings, colons before blocks, and indentation inside blocks.

Small syntax mistakes can stop a program running.
topics.syntax:
```python
if name == "Joe":
    print("Same name!")
```

topics.title: Variables
topics.summary: Named storage for a value that a program can use and change.
topics.description:
A variable can hold text, numbers, Booleans, lists, or other values. Give it a useful name so code is easy to understand.

Use the variable name without quotation marks when you want the stored value.
topics.syntax:
```python
first_name = "Alex"
print(first_name)
```

topics.title: Assignment
topics.summary: Uses `python:=` to store a value in a variable.
topics.description:
The single equals sign assigns the value on the right to the variable name on the left.

It does **not** check whether two things are equal. Use [[equality|==]] for that.
topics.syntax:
```python
score = 10
name = "Sam"
```

topics.title: snake_case
topics.summary: A Python naming style that uses lowercase words joined with underscores.
topics.description: Variable and function names should be clear. In Python, names like `python:first_name` and `python:secret_number` are easier to read than names with spaces or capitals.
topics.syntax:
```python
favourite_food = "pizza"
secret_number = 7
```

topics.title: Data types
topics.summary: Different kinds of values, such as text, numbers, Booleans, and lists.
topics.description: Python treats different types differently. Text is a [[strings|string]], whole numbers are [[integers-floats|integers]], decimal numbers are floats, and true-or-false values are [[booleans|Booleans]].
topics.syntax:
```python
name = "Alex"      # string
age = 11           # integer
height = 1.45      # float
is_ready = True    # Boolean
```

topics.title: input()
topics.summary: Asks the user a question and returns their answer as text.
topics.description:
`python:input()` pauses the program until the user types an answer. Store the answer in a variable so the program can use it later.

`python:input()` always gives back a string, even when the user types digits.
topics.syntax:
```python
name = input("What is your name? ")
print("Nice to meet you,", name)
```

topics.title: Strings
topics.summary: Text data written between quotation marks.
topics.description:
Strings can contain letters, spaces, numbers, emojis, and symbols. Python can display them, join them, search them, and store them in variables.

A variable name in quotes is just text; a variable name without quotes uses the stored value.
topics.syntax:
```python
message = "Hello!"
print(message)
```

topics.title: Escape characters
topics.summary: Special backslash codes that let strings include awkward characters.
topics.description:
A backslash can help Python understand that the next character belongs inside the string. For example, `python:\'` can include an apostrophe inside a single-quoted string.

The escape `python:\n` creates a new line.
topics.syntax:
```python
print('I\'m learning Python!')
print("Line one\nLine two")
```

topics.title: Triple-quoted strings
topics.summary: Strings written with three quotes so they can span multiple lines.
topics.description:
Triple quotes are useful for longer text, dialogue, or text that contains both single and double quotation marks.

They can also be used as large notes, although `python:#` comments are better for ordinary comments.
topics.syntax:
```python
message = """On your marks!
Get set!
GO!"""
print(message)
```

topics.title: String concatenation
topics.summary: Combines strings together with `python:+`.
topics.description:
Concatenation joins strings end to end. Remember to include spaces yourself, because Python will not add them automatically.

If you are mixing text with numbers, convert the number with [[str|str()]] or use an [[f-strings|f-string]].
topics.syntax:
```python
first = "Big"
second = " Ben"
story = first + second
print(story)
```

topics.summary: Updates a variable by adding a new value onto its current value.
topics.description: `python:+=` is a shorter way to write `python:story = story + " more text"`. With strings it appends text. With numbers it increases the value.
topics.syntax:
```python
story = "Brown Bear"
story += " is hungry!"
print(story)
```

topics.title: len()
topics.summary: Counts how many items are in a sequence.
topics.description: Use `python:len()` to count characters in a string or items in a list. It helps loops adapt when a word or list changes length.
topics.syntax:
```python
word = "banana"
print(len(word))

names = ["Amy", "Bob", "Eve"]
print(len(names))
```

topics.title: String methods
topics.summary: Built-in actions that belong to strings and are called with dot notation.
topics.description: Methods are functions attached to an object. String methods such as `python:.upper()`, `python:.lower()`, `python:.title()`, and `python:.replace()` return changed versions of the text.
topics.syntax:
```python
greeting = "would you like a hug?"
print(greeting.upper())
print(greeting.title())
print(greeting.replace("hug", "snack"))
```

topics.title: .format()
topics.summary: Fills `python:{}` placeholders in a string with supplied values.
topics.description: The values inside `python:.format()` fill the `python:{}` placeholders from left to right. This is often clearer than building a long sentence with lots of `python:+` signs.
topics.syntax:
```python
message = "My name is {} and I live in {}"
print(message.format("Alex", "London"))
```

topics.title: F-strings
topics.summary: Strings that insert variables or expressions inside `python:{}`.
topics.description:
Put `python:f` before the opening quote, then place variable names or calculations inside curly brackets.

F-strings are useful for personalised messages and calculation results.
topics.syntax:
```python
name = "Alex"
age = 11
print(f"My name is {name} and I am {age} years old")
print(f"In five years I will be {age + 5}")
```

topics.title: Booleans
topics.summary: True-or-false values written as `python:True` or `python:False`.
topics.description: Booleans are used for questions the program can answer with yes or no. Python's Boolean values must start with capital letters: `python:True` and `python:False`.
topics.syntax:
```python
is_windy = True
has_wetsuit = False
print(is_windy)
```

topics.title: bool()
topics.summary: Converts a value into its Boolean truth value.
topics.description: `python:bool()` helps you explore truthy and falsey values. Most non-empty strings and non-zero numbers are truthy. Empty strings and zero are falsey.
topics.syntax:
```python
print(bool(1))      # True
print(bool(0))      # False
print(bool("hi"))   # True
print(bool(""))     # False
```

topics.title: in
topics.summary: Checks membership or loops through a sequence, depending on the code.
topics.description: `python:in` can ask whether a value appears inside a string or list. It also appears in `python:for` loops, where it means the loop variable should take each value from a sequence.
topics.syntax:
```python
print("ban" in "banana")

for fruit in ["apple", "banana"]:
    print(fruit)
```

topics.title: not in
topics.summary: Checks that a value is absent from a string or list.
topics.description: `python:not in` is the opposite of `python:in`. It is useful when the program should do something only if a character, word, or item is missing.
topics.syntax:
```python
vowels = ["a", "e", "i", "o", "u"]
letter = "b"
if letter not in vowels:
    print(letter, end="")
```

topics.title: and, or, not
topics.summary: Operators that combine or reverse Boolean values.
topics.description: `python:and` is true only when both sides are true. `python:or` is true when at least one side is true. `python:not` flips a Boolean to its opposite.
topics.syntax:
```python
has_permission = True
is_old_enough = False

print(has_permission and is_old_enough)
print(has_permission or is_old_enough)
print(not has_permission)
```

topics.summary: Checks whether two values are equal.
topics.description: Use `python:==` inside conditions when the program needs to compare values. Do not confuse it with [[assignment|=]], which stores a value in a variable.
topics.syntax:
```python
name = input("What is your name? ")
if name == "Joe":
    print("We have the same name!")
```

topics.title: Comparison operators
topics.summary: Operators such as `python:<`, `python:>`, `python:<=`, and `python:>=` that compare values.
topics.description:
Comparisons return Booleans. Use them to check ages, scores, temperatures, guesses, counters, and other values.

`python:>=` means greater than or equal to. `python:<=` means less than or equal to.
topics.syntax:
```python
score = 10
if score >= 8:
    print("Passed!")
else:
    print("Try again")
```

topics.title: if statements
topics.summary: Runs indented code only when a condition is true.
topics.description: An `python:if` statement lets a program make a decision. The condition goes after `python:if`, then a colon starts the indented block.
topics.syntax:
```python
is_sunny = True
if is_sunny:
    print("Go outside and play!")
```

topics.title: else
topics.summary: Runs when the previous `python:if` or `python:elif` conditions were not true.
topics.description: `python:else` is the final fallback branch. It does not need its own condition because it catches everything left over.

topics.title: elif
topics.summary: Adds another condition between `python:if` and `python:else`.
topics.description: `python:elif` means else-if. Python tests it only if the earlier condition was false. Use it when there are more than two possible outcomes.

topics.title: Indentation
topics.summary: Spaces at the start of a line that show which block the line belongs to.
topics.description: Python uses indentation for the body of `python:if`, `python:else`, `python:elif`, loops, and functions. Lines with the same indentation level belong together.
topics.syntax:
```python
for i in range(3):
    print(i)
    print("inside the loop")
print("after the loop")
```

topics.title: Integers and floats
topics.summary: Integers are whole numbers; floats are decimal numbers.
topics.description:
Integers can be positive, negative, or zero. Floats have decimal points.

Division with `python:/` returns a float, even if the answer looks like a whole number.
topics.syntax:
```python
age = 11          # integer
price = 4.99      # float
print(10 / 2)     # 5.0
```

topics.title: Arithmetic
topics.summary: Maths operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
topics.description: Python can calculate with numbers using operators. `python:/` divides and returns a float. `python://` performs floor division, which drops the decimal part.
topics.syntax:
```python
print(5 + 3)
print(10 - 2)
print(4 * 6)
print(10 / 2)
print(10 // 3)
```

topics.title: Order of operations
topics.summary: The order Python follows when calculating an expression.
topics.description:
Python follows normal maths priority: brackets first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.

Use brackets when you want to make the intended order extra clear.
topics.syntax:
```python
car_speed = 5 + 3 * 4 - 2
print(car_speed)

rating = (5 + 3) * 4
print(rating)
```

topics.title: round()
topics.summary: Rounds a number to the nearest whole number or decimal place.
topics.description: Use `python:round()` when a calculation produces more decimal detail than you want to display. It rounds to the nearest value, not always upwards.
topics.syntax:
```python
print(round(4.6))
print(round(4.234, 2))
```

topics.title: str()
topics.summary: Converts a value into a string.
topics.description: Use `python:str()` when you need to join a number with text using `python:+`. F-strings can often do this more neatly.
topics.syntax:
```python
laps = 2
print("Racing laps: " + str(laps))
```

topics.title: int()
topics.summary: Converts a suitable value into a whole number.
topics.description: `python:input()` returns text. Wrap it with `python:int()` when the user's answer should be used in a number calculation or numeric comparison.
topics.syntax:
```python
age = int(input("How old are you? "))
print(f"In five years you will be {age + 5}")
```

topics.title: float()
topics.summary: Converts a suitable value into a decimal number.
topics.description: Use `python:float()` when a text value may include a decimal point and you need to calculate with it.
topics.syntax:
```python
price = float(input("Enter the price: "))
print(price * 2)
```

topics.title: While loops
topics.summary: Repeats indented code while a condition remains true.
topics.description: A `python:while` loop is useful when the program should keep going until a condition changes. Make sure something inside the loop can make the condition become false.
topics.syntax:
```python
count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print("Hello!")
    count += 1
```

topics.title: Infinite loops
topics.summary: Loops that keep running until something stops them.
topics.description: An accidental infinite loop happens when the condition never becomes false. A planned infinite loop, such as `python:while True`, can be useful in games and menus when paired with [[break|break]].

topics.title: break
topics.summary: Stops the nearest loop immediately.
topics.description: Use `python:break` when the program has found what it needs, the player has won, the user wants to stop, or an attempt limit has been reached.
topics.syntax:
```python
while True:
    password = input("Password: ")
    if password == "python":
        print("Welcome!")
        break
```

topics.title: Counters
topics.summary: Variables that track how many times something has happened.
topics.description: Counters often start at `python:0` or `python:1` and increase or decrease inside a loop. They are useful for attempts, scores, lives, and counting matches.
topics.syntax:
```python
tries = 0
while tries < 3:
    tries += 1
    print(f"Try number {tries}")
```

topics.title: For loops
topics.summary: Repeats indented code once for each item in a sequence.
topics.description: Use a `python:for` loop when you want to repeat code for each number in a range, each item in a list, or each character in a string.
topics.syntax:
```python
for i in range(5):
    print(i)
```

topics.title: range()
topics.summary: Creates a sequence of numbers, often used by a for loop.
topics.description:
`python:range(5)` provides `python:0, 1, 2, 3, 4`. It creates five loop turns even though the final number is `python:4`.

Use start, stop, and step values when you need a custom count.

topics.title: Lists
topics.summary: Ordered collections of values written inside square brackets.
topics.description: A list can store several related values in one variable. Items are separated with commas, and string items still need quotation marks.
topics.syntax:
```python
animals = ["cat", "dog", "rabbit"]
print(animals)
```

topics.title: .append()
topics.summary: Adds a new item to the end of a list.
topics.description: Use `python:.append()` when you want to grow a list while the program runs, such as adding shopping items, guessed letters, or vowels found in a word.
topics.syntax:
```python
shopping_list = []
shopping_list.append("milk")
print(shopping_list)
```

topics.title: .remove()
topics.summary: Removes the first matching item from a list by value.
topics.description: Use `python:.remove()` when you know the item value you want to take out. If that value is not in the list, Python raises an error.
topics.syntax:
```python
pets = ["cat", "rabbit", "dog"]
pets.remove("rabbit")
print(pets)
```

topics.title: .pop()
topics.summary: Removes and returns an item from a list.
topics.description: With no index, `python:.pop()` removes the final item. With an index, it removes the item at that position. You can store the popped item in a variable.
topics.syntax:
```python
colors = ["red", "blue", "yellow"]
last_color = colors.pop()
print(last_color)
print(colors)
```

topics.title: Indexes
topics.summary: Number positions used to access items in lists or characters in strings.
topics.description:
Python indexes start at `python:0`. The first item is index `python:0`, the second is index `python:1`, and so on.

Use square brackets after the list or string to access an index.
topics.syntax:
```python
colors = ["red", "blue", "yellow"]
print(colors[0])

word = "python"
print(word[2])
```

topics.title: Negative indexes
topics.summary: Indexes that count backwards from the end of a sequence.
topics.description: `python:-1` means the final item or character. `python:-2` means the one before that. Negative indexes are handy for reading from the end of a word or list.
topics.syntax:
```python
word = "python"
print(word[-1])
print(word[-2])
```

topics.title: Looping through lists
topics.summary: Uses a loop to process each item in a list.
topics.description: A `python:for` loop can visit each list item in order. The loop variable stores the current item for one iteration.
topics.syntax:
```python
fruits = ["apple", "banana"]
for fruit in fruits:
    print(f"I love to eat {fruit}!")
```

topics.title: Looping through strings
topics.summary: Uses a loop to process each character in a string.
topics.description: Strings are sequences of characters, so a `python:for` loop can visit each letter. You can loop directly through characters or loop through indexes with `python:range(len(word))`.
topics.syntax:
```python
word = "python"
for letter in word:
    print(letter)

for i in range(len(word)):
    print(f"Letter {i} is {word[i]}")
```

topics.title: print(end=...)
topics.summary: Controls what `python:print()` adds after its output.
topics.description:
By default, `python:print()` moves to a new line. The `python:end` argument can replace that with a space, a symbol, or an empty string.

This is useful for printing word characters, hidden-word dashes, or decorated names on one line.
topics.syntax:
```python
for letter in "Daisy":
    print(letter, end="*")
```

topics.title: Functions
topics.summary: Reusable named blocks of code.
topics.description: Define a function with `python:def`, a name, brackets, a colon, and an indented body. Call the function by writing its name with brackets.
topics.syntax:
```python
def cheer():
    print("You can do it!")

cheer()
```

topics.title: Parameters and arguments
topics.summary: Parameters are placeholders in a function; arguments are the real values passed in.
topics.description:
A parameter is written in the function definition. An argument is supplied when the function is called.

Parameters let one function work with many different values.
topics.syntax:
```python
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello {name}!")

greet("Alex")
greet("Sam")
```

topics.title: Division by zero
topics.summary: An invalid division that should be checked before using `python:/`.
topics.description: Python cannot divide by zero. Check the second number before dividing so the program can print a helpful message instead of crashing.

topics.title: Menu choices
topics.summary: Lets the user choose between numbered program options.
topics.description: A menu prints available options, collects the user's choice, converts it to a number if needed, and uses conditionals to run the matching code.
topics.syntax:
```python
print("1. Add")
print("2. Subtract")
choice = int(input("Choose an option: "))

if choice == 1:
    print("Adding")
elif choice == 2:
    print("Subtracting")
else:
    print("Invalid choice")
```

topics.title: Accumulators
topics.summary: Variables or lists that collect results while a loop runs.
topics.description: An accumulator starts empty or at zero, then changes inside a loop. It can count vowels, collect guessed letters, or build a shopping list.
topics.syntax:
```python
vowels_used = []
for letter in "traffic":
    if letter in ["a", "e", "i", "o", "u"]:
        vowels_used.append(letter)
print(vowels_used)
```

topics.title: Nested loops
topics.summary: A loop placed inside another loop.
topics.description: Use nested loops when each item needs its own repeated process. For example, the outer loop can choose a name, and the inner loop can process each letter in that name.
topics.syntax:
```python
names = ["Daisy", "Alex"]
for name in names:
    print("*", end="")
    for letter in name:
        print(letter, end="*")
    print()
```

topics.title: Boolean flags
topics.summary: Boolean variables that remember whether something has happened.
topics.description: A flag usually starts as `python:False` and changes to `python:True` when an event happens. Games can use flags to remember whether the player has won or whether hidden letters remain.
topics.syntax:
```python
win = False
if guess == secret_number:
    win = True

if win == False:
    print("You lost")
```

topics.title: import
topics.summary: Loads extra code from a module so your program can use it.
topics.description: Python has modules full of useful tools. Import a module before using its functions. For random numbers, import the `python:random` module.
topics.syntax:
```python
import random
print(random.randint(1, 10))
```

topics.title: random.randint()
topics.summary: Generates a random whole number between two inclusive limits.
topics.description: Use `python:random.randint(a, b)` after importing `python:random`. The result can be any integer from `python:a` to `python:b`, including both end values.
topics.syntax:
```python
import random
secret_number = random.randint(1, 10)
```

topics.title: Replay loops
topics.summary: Outer loops that let a whole game or tool run again.
topics.description: A replay loop often uses `python:while True` around the whole game. At the end, ask whether the user wants to play again and use `python:break` if they say no.
topics.syntax:
```python
while True:
    print("Play one game here")
    again = input("Play again? ")
    if again == "no":
        break
```

topics.title: HTML elements
topics.summary: The building blocks that describe content on a web page.
topics.description: Elements usually have an opening tag, content and a closing tag. Headings and paragraphs are common examples.
topics.syntax:
`html:

Hello page!

`

topics.title: Headings
topics.summary: Titles and subheadings represented by h1 through h6 tags.
topics.description: An h1 is normally the most important heading on a page. Smaller numbered headings introduce subsections.
topics.syntax:
`html:

My Website

`

topics.title: CSS properties
topics.summary: Settings that control how selected HTML content looks.
topics.description: A property is followed by a colon, a value and a semicolon inside a CSS rule.

topics.title: CSS selectors
topics.summary: Patterns that choose which HTML elements a CSS rule styles.
topics.description: Select a tag by name, a class with a dot or an id with a hash symbol.

topics.title: background-image
topics.summary: Displays an image behind an element's content.
topics.description: Provide an image address using `css:url()`. Other background properties control its size, position and repetition.
topics.syntax: `css:background-image: url("images/photo.jpg");`

topics.title: Event blocks
topics.summary: Hat blocks that start scripts when something happens.
topics.description: A green-flag or key-pressed event starts the blocks connected beneath it.
topics.syntax: `scratch:when green flag clicked`

topics.title: Motion blocks
topics.summary: Blue blocks that move or turn a sprite on the stage.
topics.description: Sprites can move steps, turn, glide, or change their x and y positions.
topics.syntax: `scratch:move (10) steps`

topics.title: Repeat blocks
topics.summary: Control blocks that run the blocks inside them several times.
topics.description: Set the repeat number to decide how many times the nested instructions run.
topics.syntax: `scratch:repeat (10)`
